If you're putting soil in them, you may want to darken them too. Light will kill roots and it penetrates the soil an inch or so.

Looks really cool though! Really great idea!

I was wondering about that!

We plan to get some landscaping fabric and make little coozies for them, since we were worried about heat buildup.

Why do roots stunt in the presence of sunlight, I wonder?

That's cool but I'm not optimistic that it will last until harvest as is. The sun will degrade and weaken the plastic, that nylon rope is rather narrow, and the constant rocking back and forth from the wind isn't going to do it any favors. It's going to be a lot heavier when it's full of dirt and has a plant growing out of the top of it. A good storm in july will take them all out pretty easy.

Those plants can get kind of bushy too so you might want to think about putting spacers in between. Aluminum or tin cans in between would work.

I kept most of the flat bottom on the containers so that, in the case of the rope pulling through the plastic, there'd be a whole bunch of flat bottom to continue supporting their weight.

You're right that sunlight will degrade the plastic but I think the biggest danger right now is in the sharp edges fraying the rope. If that happens I'll add some duct tape.

We go through enough juice and milk that there's no shortage of containers, even if these break down by the end of the season we'll have plenty more next year!

Be cautious during really warm and cold months, the soil in the ground takes a lot longer to change temp than these containers will. Even if it's 100 out, the soil (if mulched) will probably be 65-80. These planters will probably be right around the same temp as the air around them. Plants are more sensitive to their soil conditions than their air conditions. You could honestly cook the roots of certain plants.

Thanks! That's some great practical advice.

I was planning on making a loose "hat" of black landscaping fabric, to keep the roots dark and help insulate from the sun's heat.

Pretty much everybody and their brother say they study Computer Science nowdays, or that they know how to code. I'm not from US and i don't know how things work there but from your own perspective, is that really true, Voat? i'm a 1st year Computer Science student, and while i do have a technical background, it's fucking HARD. Don't get me wrong, it's doable if you put in the study hours but you need to have a strong passion for this, it's roughly 5 1/2 years to graduate here.
Are there really that many people who study Computer Science?

Depends on the kind of people you know. I had a large group of friends in highschool, virtually all of the ones that had played videogames said they were going to study Computer Science. I'm talking at least 20 people. (I'm not attacking people who play videogames, I played them too, just stating what I observed.)

I'm not saying these people made it as a CompSci major but they definitely said that they would try. Only one of my buddies did I think would actually be successful in the field, where as everyone else's experience was "I played fallout on my PC and I have no idea what I want to do with my life but I'm sure I can make it as a CompSci major, it will be easy!"

This other guy had actually been coding apps and other programs since middle school and he was genuinely worried about how he would do in actual courses.

Yup I've seen that quite a bit too. People wanting to make video games trying to get into computer science, when in fact they don't need computer science to get into coding or video games. Computer science is the study of how and what a computer is. I've had Phd computer science professors not know a lick of code but lead successful careers in their respective field of study.

The smart ones that realize that this isn't what they signed up for end up going for CIS or computer information systems which focuses more on business computing and is more along the lines not caring about theory at all and is more focused on application, which is what the end goal ends up being for them.
Yeah, a lot of people seem to think that computer science is just programming.

Lots of people study "computer science" but its more than just coding. A vast majority of people who finish their studies are just going to be IT professionals, database administrators, etc... not coders. It would benefit them to have a background knowledge of coding of course, but most of those jobs are going to require one or two formulae thats stapled to every monitor--if even that... so its not like they'll have to reinvent the wheel.

Hell there's a lot of companies here in the U.S. where using MS Excel is considered a real skill.

If coding REALLY is your passion, by all means go for it, but if you're dreading taking more coding classes instead of being excited about them then remember there are many other jobs in computer science. Not all of them pay well, but some of them do. If you just like working with tech, but not necessarily sitting behind a computer monitor all day. Think about taking some medical technology classes radiology, ultrasound, and the million different kinds of surgical or lab techs get paid pretty good money.

Or you can just fuck up like I did, and go to school for pre-med, switch to business and come out an engineer.

outside of university, I don't know any comp sci majors.

At my uni of like 8000, there are probably only about 80 or so comp sci majors (freshmen - seniors).

We get a large batch of freshmen every fall but only about 20 of about 50 actually finish through .

A lot of people in comp sci are "gamers". there are many people who are also into anime. These are people (including myself) who grew up with computers.
Growing up with a computer for the win.. Who needs parents anyway, when you can be raised by a horde of trolls?

Yes, but it's an aptitude that can't be taught, so the amount of people who actual end up in the field is perhaps 1% of those who study it. Honestly, if you don't find it enjoyable don't waste your time, it's not for you. If it's hard but you really like it, then welcome, it gets easier, but you can never stop learning no matter how old you get, unlike most other professions.

In america it is really easy to major in something hard and not get a job when you get out. Colleges here are dumbed down to the point where they can make the maximum amount of money, while maintaining a high enough job placement rate to justify their existence (this is a major problem with for profit higher education).
For instance, I am a geology major. There are a lot of good high paying jobs in my field, and the course work is fun and involves lots of travel. Everyone I have talked to who does geology professionally has done an undergraduate research project, and people who don't get a degree, but will likely not work in the any related fields when they get out.
People who succeed, and get the jobs in difficult fields are the ones who do more than just the course work. If someone says that they are a comp sci major, ask them what their research is on. If the answer is that they don't have one, then I wouldn't put too much stock into what they say.

Most people don't know how to code. Believe me. Most people nowadays know way more about being an end user than their parents.
Programming is a mindset that some people just get and others struggle with. It will always be somewhat niche. No thanks to India (and the policies that give away our jobs) the market it pretty much saturated here.
I was a physics major and my computer programming class was the most difficult class I took outside of maybe quantum mechanics.

Lots of folks code, but didn't graduate with a cs degree. Lots of people start cs and drop. Lots of engineers code. Lots of folks are self taught html, etc.

I studied CS, hated the homework and switched majors. Got two other degrees, am a computer nerd by trade where I use programming skills along with skills from my other degreed fields.
